summary: Defines the api-catalog well-known URI and link relation to help automated discovery and use of published APIs. A request to the api-catalog resource returns a document with information and links about the publisher's APIs.

eli5.summary: A website puts a list of its helper services in a known spot, so programs can find the list without asking a person.

questions: how to discover apis on a website automatically

subtitle: A well-known address where a website lists the APIs it offers, so software can find them without a human.

tldr.problem: Before anyone can use a Publisher's APIs they must find out which APIs exist, what they are for, what the usage policies are and where each endpoint lives. Doing that by hand does not suit automated clients.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC registers the api-catalog well-known URI and the api-catalog link relation. A request to /.well-known/api-catalog returns an API catalog document in Linkset format (application/linkset+json) with links to the Publisher's API endpoints.
tldr.outcome: It is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted or updated. It gives clients one predictable place to start discovering APIs and complements, rather than replaces, existing API management frameworks.

today: RFC 9727 is a Proposed Standard published in June 2025, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on RFC 8615 for well-known URIs and RFC 9264 for the Linkset format.

sections.title: Why APIs Need a Front Door
sections.content:
An application may publish APIs so that outside parties can interact with it. Those APIs must be discovered before they can be used: the outside party needs to know which APIs a Publisher exposes, their purpose, any usage policies and the endpoint for each one. RFC 9727 proposes two things to make that discovery automatic: a well-known URI named api-catalog and a link relation, also named api-catalog.

The primary goal is automated discovery of a Publisher's public API endpoints, along with metadata about each API. The catalog is mainly machine-readable but may also link to human-readable documentation. The RFC says plainly what it does not do: it does not mandate paths for API endpoints, and it does not require them to be hosted on the same host as the catalog.
sections.eli5: Programs that want to use a company's services need a list of them. This RFC says where to put the list so that every program knows where to look.

sections.title: The Well-Known URI
sections.content:
The API catalog MUST be named api-catalog in a well-known location, as defined by RFC 8615. The Publisher decides where the catalog document really lives, and /.well-known/api-catalog is a convenient reference to that location. The URI is meant for HTTPS servers that publish APIs.

A Publisher supporting this URI SHALL resolve an HTTPS GET request to /.well-known/api-catalog and return an API catalog document. It SHALL also resolve an HTTPS HEAD request to the same path with a response that includes a Link header carrying the relation defined in the RFC.

Because the real document can be anywhere, the Publisher may serve it directly or resolve the well-known request to a file such as my_api_catalog.json.
sections.eli5: Every website keeps its list in the same cupboard with the same label. Ask the cupboard and you get the list, wherever the list is really kept.

sections.title: The api-catalog Link Relation
sections.content:
The RFC also introduces a new link relation from RFC 8288, api-catalog. Its target is a resource that lists the APIs available from the Publisher of the link context. The target may be /.well-known/api-catalog or any other URI the Publisher picks.

The Publisher can advertise it in an HTTP header, as in Link: </my_api_catalog.json>; rel=api-catalog, or in the page content with an HTML link that carries rel="api-catalog".

Inside a catalog, the item relation from RFC 6573 marks a target that is an API belonging to the catalog. Other link relations may be used to describe each API.
sections.eli5: A website can also leave a sign on its front page that says "our list of services is over here", in case the list is not in the usual cupboard.

sections.title: The API Catalog Document
sections.content:
The catalog MUST include hyperlinks to API endpoints. It is RECOMMENDED that it also include useful metadata, such as usage policies, API version information and links to OpenAPI Specification definitions. If that metadata is not in the catalog itself, the Publisher SHOULD make it available at the API endpoint URIs it lists.

The Publisher MUST publish the catalog in the Linkset format application/linkset+json from RFC 9264. The Linkset SHOULD carry a profile parameter whose Profile URI value is https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9727, to signal that it is an API catalog.

Other formats may be offered through content negotiation. A Publisher that already lists its APIs in another format and wants to use the well-known URI MUST also implement a Linkset with at least hyperlinks to the API endpoints, and MAY return its existing format by content negotiation.

A catalog can also contain links to other API catalogs, using the api-catalog relation for each link.
sections.eli5: The list has to be written in one agreed style, so every program can read it. Fancier styles are allowed too, as long as the plain one is there.

sections.title: Running a Catalog in Practice
sections.content:
If APIs are spread across several domains, the RFC RECOMMENDS publishing the well-known URI at each API domain, returning the same catalog from all of them. The Publisher should choose one instance as the canonical reference and have the others redirect to it. If another party is the domain authority for a domain that hosts some of the APIs, the catalog MAY link to that party's catalog using the api-catalog relation.

For a large number of APIs, the Publisher may group them, give each group its own catalog and use the main catalog to link to these. The Publisher SHOULD consider caching and compression to reduce network overhead.

Operational advice covers availability, performance, usage, current data (removing stale entries as part of the release lifecycle) and correct metadata (checking syntax and proofreading). The RFC also says the catalog is meant to complement API management frameworks and not replace the discovery mechanisms they already have. A Publisher may even use the URI on an internal network to point authorised users at private APIs, which brings extra security considerations.
sections.eli5: If a company has shops in many towns, every shop should show the same list or point to the main one. Keep the list tidy and up to date, and remove services that are gone.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
For all cases, TLS SHOULD be used, so the catalog is available only over HTTPS and cannot be tampered with. The Publisher SHOULD review the catalog for security and privacy before deployment so that it does not leak personal, business or other sensitive metadata. External requests, and internal systems that monitor the URI, SHOULD get read-only privileges, with write privileges limited to roles that update the catalog. Rate limiting is RECOMMENDED to help mitigate abuse and denial-of-service attacks.

For public-facing APIs, security teams SHOULD audit the catalog to be sure that APIs meant only for internal use were not included by mistake. For internal APIs, the Publisher SHOULD use controls such as Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS) policies and access control lists so only authorised roles and systems can reach the catalog.

A regularly audited catalog can also help retire "zombie" APIs, legacy APIs that should no longer be available and that are unlikely to be supported, monitored, patched or updated.
sections.eli5: A list of everything you offer is helpful, but it should not accidentally show secret doors. Check it, protect it and do not let strangers edit it.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: The RFC registers three items. The api-catalog URI suffix goes in the Well-Known URIs registry with status permanent and the IETF as change controller. The api-catalog link relation goes in the Link Relation Types registry, described as referring to a list of APIs available from the Publisher of the link context. The Profile URI https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9727, with the common name "API catalog", goes in the Profile URIs registry defined by RFC 7284.
sections.eli5: The name and the sign are written into official public lists, so nobody else uses them for something different.
